questions.q: What is the core limitation of an IP-based firewall rule that a VNet service endpoint is designed to fix?
options: IP addresses are a leaky proxy for identity — an IP can change or be reassigned, so trusting the IP alone isn't the same as trusting that traffic actually came from your own resource
IP-based rules are always slower to evaluate than VNet rules
IP-based firewall rules cannot be configured at the server level, only the database level
There is no real difference — service endpoints are purely a cosmetic Portal feature
questions.explain: A service endpoint extends the VNet's own network identity onto Azure SQL's endpoint, which is a stronger guarantee than an IP header claim.

questions.q: What are the two places that must both be configured for a service endpoint to actually work?
options: The Microsoft.Sql service endpoint enabled on the subnet, and a Virtual Network rule added on the Azure SQL server naming that VNet/subnet
Only the server's firewall page — subnet configuration is optional
Only the subnet's settings — no server-side configuration is needed
The database's row-level security policy and the server's audit settings
questions.explain: Miss either side and the feature silently doesn't restrict anything as expected.

questions.q: Does enabling a VNet service endpoint give Azure SQL a private IP address inside your VNet?
options: No — traffic still routes to Azure SQL's public endpoint, just gated by a tighter, identity-based rule instead of only an IP rule
Yes — it removes the public endpoint and replaces it with a private IP automatically
Yes, but only for Managed Instance, never for Azure SQL Database
It depends on whether Transparent Data Encryption is also enabled
questions.explain: That's exactly the distinction from Private Endpoints (Lesson 28), which do assign a private IP and remove public exposure entirely.

questions.q: What Azure CLI command configures the server-side Virtual Network rule?
options: az sql server vnet-rule create --resource-group myRG --server myserver --name allow-app-subnet --vnet-name myVNet --subnet mySubnet
az sql db audit-policy update
az network private-endpoint create
sp_set_firewall_rule directly configures VNet rules with no CLI needed
questions.explain: Virtual Network rules are configured via the Portal, CLI, or PowerShell (New-AzSqlServerVirtualNetworkRule) — not through the IP-rule stored procedure.

questions.q: If a VM sits in a subnet WITHOUT the Microsoft.Sql service endpoint enabled, but its IP happens to match an existing IP firewall rule, what happens?
options: It is still evaluated against the ordinary IP firewall rules and can connect if one of those separately permits it — the VNet rule is a separate, additional gate, not a replacement
It is always rejected regardless of any IP rule, because VNet rules override everything
It automatically gets a private endpoint connection instead
The connection succeeds only if Always Encrypted is also configured
questions.explain: VNet rules and IP rules are evaluated independently — either one matching is enough to pass the firewall stage.
